title: Ranking
idea: Ranking for AZ (Brief doc tab "ranking for AZ"). 1:1 swipe of the dentist "rates whitening trends on a scale of 1-10" TikTok, swapped to skin tags: a calm man at an office desk ranks every way people try to get rid of skin tags (freezing kits, clippers, floss, patches, getting them burned off) and ends on castor oil as his favorite. Backed by: the ranking format (dentist reference + ClarityMD's top-4 ranking, 68 days + our #303) and Johnny's launched skin tag winner #156 (angle + the "soaks into the root, ricinoleic acid cuts off the blood supply, dries out" mechanism, shown with the same #156 animation). Skin tags = our lowest-sophistication angle, so a fair, funny ranking of the painful options should land hard.

script.script:
H1 (straight in, like the reference): Freezing kits. Three. It burns, it blisters, and half the time it grows right back in the same spot.

H2 (own spoken symptom call-out): If you've got skin tags on your neck or under your arms, I'm going to rank every way people try to get rid of them. My favorite is the last one. Freezing kits. Three... can hurt pretty bad.
script.visual: Initial image (all hooks): exactly the reference's first frame (ref 0:00): him at the desk, window behind, centred, title text on top; a square photo of a generic at-home freezing kit pops up lower centre as he says "Freezing kits".
script.on_screen_text:
Rating skin tag removal methods on a scale of 1-10
(recommend the last one)
(fixed white title at the top the whole video, like the reference)

script.script: Rank 2: Cutting them off with nail clippers. Negative two. Please don't. It bleeds a lot more than you think, it can get infected, and it can scar.
script.visual: Him at the desk, slight wince (ref 0:05, the "negative four" moment). Pop-up: a pair of nail clippers.

script.script: Rank 3: Tying it off with hair or dental floss. Two. You're basically doing surgery on yourself. It can get swollen and seriously irritated, and if it gets infected, now you've got a real problem.
script.visual: Pop-up: a dental floss container. Him deadpan, small shrug (ref 0:46-0:50, the "white-out" joke delivery).

script.script: Rank 4: Skin tag removal patches. Four. Some people get them to work. Most people end up with a sticky, sore spot and the tag's still there.
script.visual: Pop-up: a sheet of small clear patches. Him tilting his head, fair (ref 0:15-0:25 delivery).

script.script: Rank 5: Getting them burned off at the dermatologist. Six. It works. But it's a couple hundred dollars, a waiting list, and a tiny scar for every single one.
script.visual: Pop-up: a clinic cautery pen on a tray (like ref 0:35-0:40, the in-office whitening photo). Him nodding, fair.

script.script: Rank 6 (ours): Castor oil. Nine. My favorite, actually.
script.visual: Pop-up: OUR real amber bottle with the rose quartz roller (Products tab), a bit bigger than the others (like ref 0:38 "Ten. It's the gold standard").

script.script: It soaks deep into the skin, all the way down to the root of the skin tag. The ricinoleic acid in it cuts off the skin tag's blood supply, so it dries out, shrinks, and falls off on its own. No pain, no bleeding, no expensive doctor visits.
script.visual: Him at the desk explaining it. Pop-up (lower centre, same size as the others): the #156 skin-tag animation playing (oil sinking in → blood supply cut off → tag drying out and shrinking).
script.on_screen_text: "SOAKS DOWN TO THE ROOT" · "CUTS OFF THE BLOOD SUPPLY"

script.script: The one I'd use is Haven and Spool. It's organic, cold-pressed and hexane-free, it comes in dark amber glass, and it has a rose quartz roller, so you just roll it on the skin tag before bed and let it work while you sleep. Give it a few weeks.
script.visual: Him at the desk. Pop-up: a real-looking clip of a hand rolling our roller onto a small skin tag on the side of a neck at night, oil sheen; then back to our bottle photo.

script.script: They're doing buy one, get one free right now, and you can try it for thirty nights or it's free. Link's below.
script.visual: Him at the desk, points down (natural, not salesy). Pop-up: two of our bottles.
script.on_screen_text: BUY 1 GET 1 FREE · 30 NIGHTS OR IT'S FREE · link below

editing_notes:
Replicate this format exactly: Reference (link above). The dentist "rates whitening trends on a scale of 1-10" TikTok, swapped to skin tags.

STRUCTURE (copy the reference rhythm): fixed white title at the top the whole video (ref 0:00-1:15). For every item he says the name, the score, 1-2 lines. 4 to 8 s per item, about 60 s total. A square image of each method pops up lower centre, same size and spot as the reference (ref 0:00 the LED kit, 0:05 charcoal toothbrush, 0:10 baking soda box). Use real-looking, unbranded photos for the other methods (no competitor brands/logos). Our item gets OUR real product photo (Products tab), a bit bigger.

NO B-ROLL CUT-AWAYS: JUST like the reference. He is on camera the whole time; the only other visual is the square pop-up lower centre for each item. Every pop-up is based on a real photo or clip (a real freezing kit, real nail clippers, a real neck with small skin tags, real hands). Skin tags in pop-ups: real skin texture, small and realistic, not gross or exaggerated.

THE MECHANISM SHOT: on the castor oil line, the SAME animation as Johnny's #156 (the skin tag with the oil sinking in, the blood supply getting cut off, the tag drying out and shrinking) plays INSIDE the pop-up square (same spot and size as the other pop-ups) while he explains it. Ask Max / Pod 1 for the #156 animation file and reuse it, or rebuild it from the #156 ad frame for frame. 5-6 s.

CAPTIONS: like the reference: the score big when he says it ("NEGATIVE TWO.", "NINE."), key words white, centred low.
HOOKS: H1 = straight into "Freezing kits. Three." (like the reference). H2 = his own spoken symptom call-out first, then the same list.
OFFER: Buy 1 Get 1 Free + 30 nights or it's free (both real). Landing page: Skin Tags page.
CLAIMS: the "cuts off the blood supply... dries out and falls off" line is Johnny's launched wording (#156), but it's a removal claim. Softer back-up line if Meta rejects it: "...so it dries out and shrinks on its own." Never say it treats or cures anything.
Doc: Brief H+S, tab "ranking for AZ".

Voiceover: His own voice, deadpan and quick, exactly the reference's rhythm: item. score. one or two honest lines. A little dry humour on the bad ones (like the ref's "just buy White-Out"). NEEDS TO HAVE CONVICTION in their voice, its boring to listen to a dull script. They need to speak with character.

Avatar: One man, late 30s to 40s, clean-cut, light blue button-up shirt, seated at an office desk with a big window and city view behind him, a cork board on the wall: framed EXACTLY like the reference (waist up, centred, tripod, eye level; ref 0:00). Build every shot of him in Genjitsu with the reference video as the motion reference, so his head tilts, shrugs, hand gestures and pauses copy the reference 1:1 (ref 0:00-1:15). He looks like an expert because of the setting and the way he talks, NOT because of a title: no white coat, no scrubs, no stethoscope, no name badge, never says "Dr" or "as a doctor" (a fake credential = FTC/Meta risk). The title text says "rates", never "Doctor rates".
